1037.title: One tree, one week
1037.hook: visit the same tree daily, and let one tree teach you how much changes in a week
1037.carry: something ordinary becomes someone you visit
1037.howItsDone: Some people keep a practice of returning to the same tree or spot outdoors over days or seasons, noticing how it changes; trees also appear as images of rootedness in the Psalms and as the place of awakening in Buddhist tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was panta rhei, everything flows, and your line was never the same: clouds that never repeat. Today, something that stays put.

There's probably a tree you pass without seeing it. On the way to the bus, outside the office window, at the corner where the dog always stops. It's easy to know a phone's lock screen better than that tree. That's not a flaw; it's how attention works. What stays still, people stop looking at. Clouds get the eye because they move. A tree seems to do nothing at all. So today, not a new tree, not a famous one. The same one, every day, for a week.
screen: `THE TREE YOU PASS.` → `WHAT STAYS STILL, WE STOP SEEING.` → `THE SAME ONE, EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the tree that seems to stand still. Over a week a tree is busy: a bud swells, a leaf turns, a branch holds a bird on Monday and is empty on Tuesday, the light hits it from a new angle as the season tips. You won't see it in one glance. You'll see it by coming back. Second, trees in the old texts. The very first psalm has a tree in it. The person who delights in the law, the psalm says, "shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season." In his season: not a tree that fruits all year, but one that keeps its own time, and stays rooted while it waits. Third, the tree as a place to sit. Buddhist tradition tells of Siddhartha sitting beneath a tree, resolved not to get up until he understood, and awakening there. That tree became known as the bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. In the story, the tree doesn't teach him anything. It simply holds still while he does. Fourth, why one tree and not many. A walk in the woods is wonderful, but it's a sampler. One tree is a relationship. By day three you know where the bark is torn. By day five you notice the same branch catches the evening light. Something ordinary becomes someone you visit, and that shift, from scenery to a companion, is a small doorway into awe.
screen: `A TREE ONLY SEEMS TO STAND STILL.` · `PSALM 1: A TREE BY THE WATER.` · `THE TREE OF AWAKENING.` · `ONE TREE IS A RELATIONSHIP.` · then, large: `IN HIS SEASON.`

segments.voice: Find a tree through a window or a doorway, or step outside to one; if none is near, choose one you know well from memory. Look at it as if you'll be asked to draw it tomorrow: the shape of the trunk, where the biggest branch leaves it, the light on the leaves or the bare twigs. You don't need to think anything about it; just meet it, and let your breathing slow.
One tree. The same tree, visited day after day, until something you walked past becomes something you know. Today's word.
Your line: something ordinary becomes someone you visit. The psalm's tree keeps its own time, so there's no hurry. See you tomorrow.

1038.title: Small things up close
1038.hook: a leaf, an insect, frost: the world gets bigger the closer you look
1038.howItsDone: Poets, naturalists and contemplatives in several settings practice close looking at small living things; Blake's Auguries of Innocence and Jesus's words about the lilies in Matthew 6 are two texts that point the eye downward.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was one tree, and your line was something ordinary becomes someone you visit. Today, closer still: past the branch, to the leaf.

A frosted car window on a cold morning. The usual move is to scrape it off and drive. But lean in first, and the frost isn't a white smear at all. It's ferns. Feathers. Tiny branching forests, grown in the dark while you slept. The same goes for the veins on a leaf, the legs of a beetle, the rings of a cut onion. Awe is often filed under big things: mountains, oceans, stars. Today it goes the other way. The world gets bigger the closer you look.
screen: `FROST ON A WINDOW.` → `FERNS, FEATHERS, FORESTS.` → `BIGGER THE CLOSER YOU LOOK.`

segments.voice: First, a poet's grain of sand. William Blake, the English poet, opens his poem Auguries of Innocence with two lines: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower." He isn't saying sand is pretty. He's saying the whole is folded into the very small, if you have eyes for it. Second, a teacher's flowers. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus points his listeners to the plants at their feet: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." Then he says that Solomon, in all his glory, was not dressed like one of these. A king's robes, outshone by a wild flower. The word is consider. Not glance: stay with it. Third, why small works. Something huge can overwhelm you; you stand back from it. Something small invites you in. You have to bend down, slow down, get quiet, and that posture, low and close and still, is half the practice already. Fourth, what it changes. Spend a minute with the veins of one leaf, and a whole tree is never quite a green blur again. The detail stays with you. And small things are everywhere: on the windowsill, in the sidewalk crack, on the back of your own hand. You don't need a trip to find awe. You need to bend down.

segments.voice: Bring one small thing close, a leaf, a crumb, a drop of water on a glass, the back of your own hand, and look at its edges, then its surface, then the lines and grains and tiny colors inside it. When your mind wanders, come back to one detail. If you pray, let this be a way of attending to what's made; if you don't, simply look.
Solomon. The king Jesus named when pointing to the lilies of the field, outshone by a wild flower: bend down, look long, and the small thing opens. Today's word.
Your line: up close. Even a crumb has edges worth a second look. Day one thousand thirty-eight, done.

1039.title: Sit by water
1039.hook: ocean, lake or river: sit beside moving water and let it do the talking
1039.howItsDone: Some people seek out places by water for rest and reflection; Psalm 23 pictures being led beside still waters, and the Tao Te Ching holds up water as an image of the highest good.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Solomon, a king outshone by a wild flower, and your line was up close. Today, back out, beside something that never holds still.

A bench at the edge of a lake. One person has a coffee going cold. Another has a phone face down on her knee. Nobody is talking. They're just watching the water move against the stones, and none of them seems in a hurry to leave. For some people, water does something. A river, a harbor, a pond in a city park, the sea. Shoulders drop. Breathing slows. Nobody has to explain why.
screen: `A BENCH BY A LAKE.` → `NOBODY IN A HURRY.` → `SIT BY WATER.`

segments.voice: First, the shepherd's water. Psalm Twenty-three is a song about being cared for, and one of the first things the shepherd does is lead the sheep to water. In the King James wording: "he leadeth me beside the still waters." Not into a rushing current; beside still water. The psalm places rest right at the water's edge. Second, the book that praised water. The Tao Te Ching, the old Chinese book of the Way, uses water as a picture of the highest good. In Legge's translation, chapter eight says the highest excellence is like that of water. Water, it goes on, benefits everything without striving, and settles in the low places people avoid. It does good without competing for the high ground. Third, what sitting does. Moving water keeps changing, yet it doesn't feel restless to watch: the surface changes, the sound stays steady. Some people find that a mind which won't quiet in a room will quiet beside a stream. You don't have to make it happen. The water sets the pace. Fourth, the water you have. Not everyone lives near a coast. But water is closer than it seems: a fountain, a gutter after rain, a bathtub filling, a glass on the table catching light. The psalm doesn't say the waters were grand. It says they were still, and close enough to sit beside.
screen: `PSALM 23: BESIDE THE STILL WATERS.` · `THE TAO: THE HIGHEST GOOD IS LIKE WATER.` · `THE WATER SETS THE PACE.` · `THE WATER YOU HAVE.` · then, large: `BESIDE THE STILL WATERS.`

segments.voice: Sit beside water if you're near it; if not, run a tap slowly into a bowl, set a full glass in front of you, or remember a place by water you've loved. Watch the surface or listen to it, and let your breath follow its pace. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's line, he leadeth me beside the still waters; if you don't, let the water do the talking.
Still waters. The psalm's picture of rest at the water's edge: ocean, lake, river or a bowl from the tap, sitting beside it to slow you down. Today's word.
Your line: by water. Even a running tap can set the pace for a breath. Until tomorrow.

1040.title: Storms from safety
1040.hook: thunder and wind, heard from a safe place, can be awe instead of fear
1040.howItsDone: In the Bible, Psalm 29 hears the voice of the LORD in the thunder, and Elijah hears a still small voice after wind, earthquake and fire; some people make a quiet practice of listening to storms from a safe place.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was still waters, and your line was by water. Today the water isn't still at all. It's coming down sideways.

Hail drums on a car roof. The driver has pulled in under a gas station canopy and switched off the engine. Nobody can hear the radio. Across the road, the gutters have turned into streams and the trees are bending almost flat. Ten minutes ago, out on the highway, this storm was a gray wall and two hands tight on the wheel. Now, under a roof, it's something to watch. That's the strange thing about storms: the safer you are, the more of their size you can take in.
screen: `HAIL ON A CAR ROOF.` → `UNDER THE CANOPY.` → `THE SAFER YOU ARE, THE MORE YOU SEE.`

segments.voice: First, a storm with a voice in it. Psalm twenty-nine listens to a thunderstorm and calls the thunder a voice. In the King James words: "The voice of the LORD is upon the waters: the God of glory thundereth." The voice breaks the cedars and shakes the wilderness. In this song, the storm itself is where the voice speaks. Second, a storm with no voice in it. In the First Book of Kings, the prophet Elijah, worn out and hiding in a cave, is told to stand on the mountain. A great wind tears at the rocks, "but the LORD was not in the wind." Then an earthquake, then a fire, and the LORD was not in those either. And after the fire, "a still small voice." Third, both at once. These two texts don't cancel each other. In one, the storm is where the voice speaks; in the other, the voice comes after the storm has passed. A storm can be a messenger, or the loud thing that makes the quiet afterward audible. Fourth, why safety matters. Awe sits close to fear. Out in a real storm, fear wins; the body is busy surviving. Give it a roof, a window, a blanket, and there's room for the other feeling: how vast the sky is, how small a house is, how much power moves through a single gust.

segments.voice: Listen to rain or wind from somewhere safe and dry, by a window open a crack or at the door; if it's calm out, play a recording of a storm, or remember one you heard from inside. Notice how each gust swells and fades, and then the quiet underneath it. If you pray, you can listen for the still small voice; if you don't, let the storm be big while you are safe.
Elijah. The prophet who heard no voice in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but a still small voice after the storm had passed. Today's word.
Your line: the storm. From under a roof, it's big and you're safe, both at once. That's day one thousand forty.

1041.title: Music that moves
1041.hook: music can stop a person in the middle of a day: listen to one piece all the way through
1041.howItsDone: Music is part of worship and devotion on several paths, from psalms and hymns to Sufi poetry and kirtan; some people make a practice of listening to one piece of music fully, without doing anything else.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Elijah, and your line was the storm, heard from somewhere safe. Today, a sound people make on purpose.

A song comes on in a grocery store, and for no reason anyone else can see, someone in the cereal aisle has to stop and hold the shelf. It's a song from a wedding, or a funeral, or a car ride years ago. Three notes in, and they're somewhere else. Music turns up in temples and churches and gurdwaras, at weddings and wakes, on kitchen radios and in headphones on the night bus. And yet it's often just background. Today, music in the foreground: one piece, all the way through.
screen: `A SONG IN THE CEREAL AISLE.` → `THREE NOTES IN.` → `ONE PIECE, ALL THE WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: First, a harp in a troubled room. In the First Book of Samuel, King Saul is tormented by what the text calls an evil spirit. His servants send for a young shepherd who can play the harp. His name is David. When the trouble came on Saul, the text says, David played, and Saul was refreshed and was well, and the evil spirit left him. The story doesn't explain how. It just says the music helped. Second, a reed that cries. The Masnavi, the long poem of the Persian mystic Rumi, opens with a reed flute. The reed was cut from its reed bed, the poem says, and that's why its song sounds like longing: it's crying to go home. Some readers have heard the reed as the human soul, separated from its source, and every song as a kind of homesickness. Third, everything that breathes. In the King James Bible, the Book of Psalms ends with a psalm full of music: trumpet, harp, timbrel, strings, organs, loud cymbals. Then the last verse: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Breath itself, turned into song. Fourth, why the whole piece. A clip gives you the mood. The whole piece gives you the journey: where it starts, where it wanders, how it comes home. Listening to the end, without skipping, is a small act of trust. You let someone else's sound carry you, and see where you land.
screen: `DAVID'S HARP FOR SAUL.` · `RUMI'S REED: A SONG OF LONGING.` · `PSALM 150: EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.` · `THE WHOLE PIECE IS A JOURNEY.` · then, large: `LET EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.`

segments.voice: Choose one piece of music, a hymn, a chant, a song from your childhood, something with no words at all, then put it on and do nothing else. Follow one thread, a voice, a drum, a single instrument, and if you like, let it play past the bell to its last note. If you pray, music can be part of that; if you don't, simply let it carry you.
Masnavi. Rumi's long poem that opens with a reed flute longing for home, alongside a harp for a troubled king and a psalm of breath. Today's word.
Your line: the music. Three notes can carry a person a long way. One thousand forty-one days now.

1042.title: A newborn
1042.hook: a new person in the world: hold or picture a baby and let the newness land
1042.howItsDone: Several traditions mark a birth with blessings, naming ceremonies and prayers of thanks; Luke's account of the shepherds and Mary, and Gibran's words on children in The Prophet, are two texts that look at a new life with wonder.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Masnavi, Rumi's poem of the reed, and your line was the music. Today, a smaller sound: the first cry of someone new.

A hospital corridor at three in the morning. Behind one door, a room that held two people an hour ago now holds three. Someone small is crying, and nobody in the room minds at all. Tiny fingers. A face nobody has seen before, anywhere, ever. A person who was not in the world yesterday, and now is. Grown-ups who were exhausted a minute ago go quiet and stare. They aren't looking at a problem to solve. They're looking at something brand new.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `A FACE NOBODY HAS SEEN BEFORE.` → `SOMETHING BRAND NEW.`

segments.voice: First, a mother who kept quiet. In the Gospel of Luke, shepherds come in from the fields to see a newborn lying in a manger, and they spread the word about what they'd been told of this child. In the King James words: "all they that heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." The hearers wonder. The mother keeps it, and ponders. Second, a poet's warning. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran's book of short teachings, a woman holding a baby asks about children. The answer begins: "Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself." Parents may give their children love, Gibran goes on, but not their thoughts, because children have thoughts of their own. A newborn isn't a copy. It's someone new. Third, why a baby stops people. Much of a day is things met before: the same roads, the same faces, the same news. A newborn is plain proof that the world is still making new things. Not new products. New people, with their own faces and their own thoughts to come. Fourth, the baby you once were. Not everyone has a baby to hold, and for some people the subject is tender. But whoever is listening was once that new: unknown, unnamed. The newness in that room was, once, yours.
screen: `LUKE 2: MARY PONDERED.` · `GIBRAN: LIFE'S LONGING FOR ITSELF.` · `PROOF THE WORLD STILL MAKES NEW THINGS.` · `THE BABY YOU ONCE WERE.` · then, large: `PONDERED IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: If there's a baby in your arms, just look; if not, picture one, a child you know, a photo, or yourself on your first day, small and unnamed. Notice the hands, the tiny nails, the quick, shallow breathing, and let the newness land. If you pray, you can keep this moment the way Mary did and ponder it; if you don't, stay with the wonder of someone new.
A newborn. A person who wasn't in the world yesterday: something to ponder, in Luke's telling, and nobody's copy, in Gibran's. Today's word.
Your line: new. Every face you know was once a face nobody had seen. Day one thousand forty-two, complete.

1043.title: Sacred buildings
1043.hook: cathedral, mosque, temple, gurdwara, synagogue: visit as a respectful guest
1043.howItsDone: Churches, mosques, temples, gurdwaras and synagogues often welcome respectful visitors; guests typically dress modestly, follow the house customs on shoes and head coverings, and ask before taking photos.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a newborn, and your line was new. Today the week ends inside a building made for awe.

A heavy door swings shut behind you, and the street noise is gone. The ceiling is higher than it needs to be. Somewhere, someone is praying quietly, and you lower your voice without being asked. Cathedral, mosque, temple, gurdwara, synagogue: people have built rooms like this on purpose. You don't have to share the faith of a place to honor its hush. You only have to come in the way a guest comes into someone's home.
screen: `THE DOOR SWINGS SHUT.` → `A CEILING HIGHER THAN IT NEEDS TO BE.` → `COME IN AS A GUEST.`

segments.voice: First, a place that turned out to be holy. In Genesis, Jacob is on the run, sleeping in the open with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven, and when he wakes he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Then: "this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." There's no building yet. Just a man waking up to where he is. Second, watching your step. Ecclesiastes advises anyone entering a house of worship, in the King James words: "Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear." Holy places often ask something of the body first: shoes off in some, heads covered in others, voices lowered. The body learns respect before the mind has words for it. Third, being a guest. A sacred building is someone's spiritual home. A guest doesn't need to believe what the hosts believe, or pretend to. A guest dresses with care, asks at the door what's expected, watches what others do, and doesn't photograph people at prayer without asking. Some places welcome visitors at set hours, or have someone who will show you around. Fourth, what a guest receives. You may not pray there, or understand everything you see. But you'll stand where other people have brought their joys and griefs, and some visitors say they can feel that weight in the room. Jacob's words fit many first visits: a place that meant more than it looked, and I knew it not.
screen: `JACOB: AND I KNEW IT NOT.` · `ECCLESIASTES: KEEP THY FOOT.` · `A GUEST IN SOMEONE'S HOME.` · `WHAT A GUEST RECEIVES.` · then, large: `THE GATE OF HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Find a picture of the inside of one sacred building, a cathedral, a mosque, a temple, a gurdwara, a synagogue, and look slowly: which way do people face, where does the eye go first, where would you stand if you walked in? If you pray, let this be a quiet greeting to the place; if you don't, simply stand there as a guest.
Sacred buildings. Rooms made on purpose to change how you stand and speak, visited not as a tourist, but as a guest. Today's word.
Your line: as a guest. Seven days of awe: a tree, small things, water, a storm, music, a newborn, a sacred room. That's the week.
